cues.text: Let us turn now to a case that pulls together many of the ideas we have been building: the FinTech Nexus case.
Before we begin, a note on what kind of material this is.
It is an educational case.
That means it is a teaching scenario, written to help us practise analysis.
It is not an audited company report, and we should treat it accordingly.
The case describes a Nigerian fintech.
A fintech, short for financial technology company, is a business that uses digital technology to deliver financial services such as payments, savings, or lending.
This particular company serves underserved customers.

Underserved customers are people and small businesses that traditional banks have not reached well, perhaps because branches are far away, requirements are hard to meet, or products were not designed with them in mind.
So the company has a clear and meaningful market, and yet, as the case tells us, its growth was held back.
Let us go through the obstacles one at a time, because each one is a different kind of problem.
First, a traditional banking hierarchy.
This means decisions moved up and down a rigid chain of command, which slows learning and makes it hard to respond quickly to customers.
Second, managerial resistance.
Some managers resisted change.
This is common, because new ways of working can feel like a threat to authority, routine, or status.
Third, siloed teams.
A silo is a team that works in isolation, with its own goals, information and habits.
When teams are siloed, knowledge does not flow, and customers feel the gaps.
Fourth, inconsistent customer experience.
Because the teams were not joined up, customers did not get the same quality of service from one interaction to the next.
Fifth, weak alignment.
Alignment means that strategy, structure, people and daily work all point in the same direction.
Here, that alignment was weak.
Notice how these five obstacles reinforce one another.
A rigid hierarchy encourages silos, silos produce inconsistent experiences, and resistant managers protect the old arrangement.
That is why a single fix would not be enough.
Now let us look at the response.
The case lists several elements, and I will take them in the order given.
The first is adhocracy-oriented experimentation and employee ownership.
Adhocracy is a culture type, from the competing values framework, that values innovation, risk taking and adaptability.
Instead of waiting for permission from above, people are encouraged to try ideas, learn from results, and take ownership of outcomes.
Experimentation means testing ideas on a small scale to learn quickly.
The second is cross-functional collaboration.
This means bringing people from different functions, such as product, technology, operations and customer support, to work together on shared goals.
It is the direct answer to siloed teams.
The third is digital skills training.
Technology and new ways of working only help if people are able to use them, so the organisation invested in building those capabilities.
The fourth is digital champions.
These are employees who advocate for digital ways of working, support colleagues, and help the change spread within their own teams.
The fifth is Kotter-based change management.
This refers to John Kotter's change model, which is a structured, step-by-step approach to leading change.
It includes creating urgency, building a guiding coalition, communicating a vision, empowering action, and making change stick.
It speaks directly to managerial resistance, because it treats change as something that must be led deliberately.
The sixth is Agile development.
Agile means building products in short cycles, gathering feedback often, and adjusting as you learn, rather than planning everything in advance and delivering it at the end.
The seventh is customer-focused mobile UX.
UX, or user experience, is how it feels for a person to use a product.
Mobile matters because many underserved customers reach financial services through their phones.
Designing around the customer's needs addresses the inconsistent experience we saw earlier.
Now the results.
The case reports three figures.
A 40% improvement in user retention.
A 30% increase in employee satisfaction.
And a 25% shorter time to market.
Retention is how many users keep using the service over time.
Employee satisfaction is how positively staff feel about their work.
Time to market is how long it takes to move a product from idea to launch.
Here is the important caution.
These are case-reported figures.
They are not independently verified measurements.
So when you see numbers like these, ask questions.
What was the baseline, meaning the starting level that the improvement is measured from?
Over what period was the change measured?
And are the percentages relative?
A relative percentage compares the change to the starting value, so a rise from ten to fourteen is forty percent relative, but only four percentage points in absolute terms.
Without that information, the figures are suggestive, not conclusive.
Finally, consider what the case does and does not show.
The intervention combines four things: leadership, culture, processes and technology.
Results cannot be credited to any one of them alone, because they were changed together.
And the case is not evidence that controls should disappear in financial services.
Financial services are regulated and carry real risks to customers' money and data.
The lesson is that experimentation, speed and customer focus can be pursued alongside strong controls, not instead of them.
So, to bring it together: a Nigerian fintech serving underserved customers was held back by hierarchy, resistance, silos, inconsistent experience and weak alignment.
It responded with culture, collaboration, skills, champions, structured change, Agile delivery and mobile design.
It reports encouraging results, which we should read critically, and which show that digital transformation is a combined effort of leadership, culture, processes and technology.
